hints: Look at what has to change, you start with one OH group and need two OH groups on neighbouring carbons, so what must form in between?
Remember that an alcohol can be dehydrated to an alkene by heating strongly with Al2O3, giving cyclohexene here.
Think about how a C=C double bond is gently oxidised to add two OH groups across it without breaking the ring.
walkthrough:
**Spot the overall change**

Think like a builder. You start with cyclohexanol with one $\text{-OH}$ group. You finish with cyclohexane-1,2-diol with two $\text{-OH}$ groups on adjacent carbons.

You cannot add an $\text{-OH}$ directly. You need to go via an alkene intermediate, cyclohexene.

**Step 1, dehydrate the alcohol to an alkene**

Secondary alcohols like cyclohexanol lose water when heated strongly with aluminium oxide, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, which acts as a dehydrating catalyst.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{OH} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So step 1 must be heat strongly with $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ to make cyclohexene.

**Step 2, mild oxidation of alkene to diol**

Cold, dilute acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ gives mild oxidation across the $\text{C=C}$ bond. It adds one $\text{-OH}$ to each carbon of the double bond.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} + [\text{O}] + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow[\text{dilute}]{\text{cold KMnO}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}(\text{OH})_2$$
That product is exactly cyclohexane-1,2-diol. Hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ would cleave the ring, so cold and dilute conditions are essential.

**Put the two steps together**

dehydration to cyclohexene. Step 2: hydroxylation to the 1,2-diol. That matches the combination of heating with $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ followed by cold dilute $\text{KMnO}_4$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.

options.A: Correct. Heating cyclohexanol strongly with Al2O3 dehydrates it to cyclohexene. Cold dilute KMnO4 with H2SO4 then adds two OH groups across the double bond to give cyclohexane-1,2-diol. Both reagents and conditions are ideal for this route.
options.B: Step 1 is correct to make cyclohexene, but step 2 is wrong. Heating an alkene with steam and H2SO4 is hydration, which adds only one OH group to make cyclohexanol again, not a diol. You need oxidation, not hydration, to get two OH groups.
options.C: Step 2 is correct for alkene to diol, but step 1 is wrong. Reflux with ethanolic NaOH is used for dehydrohalogenation of a haloalkane to an alkene, not for dehydration of an alcohol. Cyclohexanol will not form cyclohexene under these basic conditions.
options.D: Both steps are wrong for this starting material. Ethanolic NaOH does not dehydrate alcohols, so no cyclohexene forms. Even if it did, steam with H2SO4 would only hydrate the alkene back to a single alcohol, never to a 1,2-diol.
